To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the dynamics of currents is essential in obtaining a reasonable agreement between models.
the agreement between models is good when the same forcing is used and the system dynamics is well known.
the dynamics of water circulation is essential for a good model agreement, and that the model harmonization process is a key step to reach a satisfactory agreement.
In summary, our research is concerned with
modelling of radionuclide dynamics in the marine environment.
the study of marine dispersion and accumulation processes of (137)Cs in the Baltic Sea after the Chernobyl nuclear accident in 1986.
the development of a new generation of operational models for marine radionuclides dispersion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the state-of-the-art of modelling of marine radionucldide dispersion is good, but the complexity of the problem is high and the development of models for decision-making is still a challenge.
the modelling of marine dispersion in a dynamic system is a complex task, requiring the development of specific modelling tools and approaches.

, in spite of the fact that the state of the art of dispersion models has reached a high level, it is still difficult to obtain reliable results for complex marine environments, especially for long-term predictions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the models used in the IAEA MODARIS project are useful tools for decision-making in case of a nuclear accident in the marine environment.
a good agreement between the models can be obtained only if they are forced with the same circulation data and the same model parameterization, but this is not enough.

, although there are some difficulties to obtain good model agreement in dynamic environments, it is possible to achieve this by using a harmonization approach and that, once the model is validated, it can be used for decision-making purposes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of a model to be used in decision-making should be based on the definition of the objectives of its use.
, for the case of Fukushima and other similar cases, the use of a single model to simulate the dispersion of radionuclides in the environment is not recommended.
a harmonization of the modelling approach is required for the post-emergency phase.
